title: Toss diced potato in a saute pan
instruction: Toss the diced potatoes in the saute pan to turn them over, without touching the food, then set the pan back on the burner.
context: Tossing food in a pan is a familiar home-cooking move: browning diced potatoes, mushrooms or vegetables in a skillet, a home cook turns them with a flick of the pan instead of a spatula, and the move is a staple of cooking shows and recipe videos. One hand on the handle slides the food to the far wall and flicks it up and back, so it lands turned without a utensil and without leaving the pan. It is a dynamic, non-prehensile skill with many loose pieces at once: nothing is grasped except the handle, and the result depends on the timing and size of one fast motion. This is not the board's spatula-flipped egg (TK-84YE4P): there is no utensil, the hand never goes near the food, and touching it zeroes the trial.
setup: Positions in cm from the midpoint between the arm bases (x forward, y left), heights above the table. A cold portable hotplate, a black steel housing 24 x 24 x 4 cm with a flat top, is fixed with its centre at x 57.1, y 3.9, turned 25 degrees clockwise seen from above. On it stands an 8 in aluminium saute (fry) pan with a bare, uncoated cooking surface, 463 g: rim 20.3 cm across inside, flat floor 13.4 cm across, a 2 cm corner radius, sides sloping out 30 degrees from vertical, 4.0 cm deep, 3 mm thick. Its handle is a flat 2.5 cm aluminium strap, 19 cm long, riveted just under the rim and rising 20 degrees, with a red silicone sleeve (13 x 3.0 x 1.8 cm) over its outer end; it points back at the left arm's base (x 0, y 30.5), ending at x 31.8, y 15.7, 14.2 cm above the table. In the pan lie twelve 13 mm dice standing in for diced par-cooked potato: cubes of natural HDPE cutting-board sheet, about 2 g each, each with one face marked dark brown, every die marked face down so that none shows from above: four in a ring 1.8 cm from the centre and eight in a ring 4.7 cm from it, as in the screenshot. No utensil is on the table. The arms start at their ready pose with open grippers. Real trial: a Vollrath Wear-Ever 400880 pan with an uncoated natural-finish aluminium cooking surface, washed and dry, no oil; the dice are 1/2 in HDPE cubes accepted by a tilt test (slide at 17 to 21 degrees on the pan floor) and a drop test (about 1 cm rebound from 10 cm), laid marked face down; the pan and burner are cold. For the toss check a phone on a stand 1 m to the side of the burner, square to the handle's line, lens about 25 cm above the burner top, records at 120 fps or more with the whole pan in frame.
scoring: Scored once at the end of the trial from a photo taken straight down into the pan, a count, and the trial video. Turned: a die at rest inside the pan whose browned face is not underneath it. Numerically, the browned face's outward normal points no lower than 30 degrees below horizontal; a die lying flat has that face down (not turned), on a side or up (turned), so only a die propped on another die or on the wall needs the angle read, with a protractor on a side photo. Lost: a die that touched the table, the burner or the floor at any time, even if it got back into the pan, or that is not inside the pan at the end (on the rim, the handle or the robot). Net = dice turned (lost dice never count as turned) minus dice lost. The score is 0 if any part of either arm or gripper touched any die at any time (real trial: from the video; simulation: a contact force between a robot link and a die reported by the physics engine, never a distance). The score is also 0 unless a toss was seen: at some moment at least 3 dice in the air over the pan at once, each with its centre above the plane of the rim (real trial: frame by frame in a 120 fps side video, more than half of each die above the rim line; simulation: each control step, die centres in the pan's frame above the rim's plane and within its circle). Otherwise: net 0-2: 0; net 3-4: 0.2; net 5-6: 0.4; net 7 or more: 0.6. With net 7 or more, 0.8 if at the end the pan stands on the burner (pan centre within 3 cm of the burner's centre, cooking surface within 5 degrees of level, base flat on the burner top), both grippers' fingertips are 8 cm or more from the pan and its handle, and the pan and dice have not moved for the last 1 s; and 1.0 if in addition no die is lost. So doing nothing, or lifting and replacing the pan, scores 0, and putting the pan back earns nothing unless the food was turned. A cube has six faces: dice that tumble at random end browned face down one time in six, so a perfect tumble turns 10 of 12 on average and the top band asks for 7. Dice do not tumble unless they leave the pan floor: measured in simulation, a hard level back-and-forth shake (pan at 0.7 m/s, five bursts) turned 3 of 12 but never lifted a die centre above 13.2 mm (the rim is at 40 mm), so it scores 0, and the scripted demo's five tosses put 3 to 10 dice above the rim at once each time and turned 11 of 12 with none lost (1.0); five more episodes with the toss changed by up to 7%, run before the toss rule, turned 10 to 12, one of them losing a die.
reset_notes: Stand the pan back on the burner with its handle on the marked line and lay the twelve dice marked face down on their spots with tongs. Real trial: wipe the pan dry if it was touched; replace a die that has chipped or lost its mark with a spare from the same sheet.
fidelity: Pan, 12 dice, burner and grippers are rigid bodies in real contact; the pan is held by finger friction alone. True sizes and masses (463 g pan; 13 mm HDPE stand-in dice, 2.1 g). Real dice are 12.7 mm with lightly broken edges; simulated ones are identical sharp cubes. HDPE on dry uncoated aluminium: friction 0.35/0.30, restitution 0.30, checked on the real dice by a tilt and a drop test. No oil, starch, heat or breakage. The marked face is painted.
scores: Demo: 1.0 at step 540 of 1,200; level shake: 0. Dream-1: 0.0 at the 1,200-step limit on the prior task.py (same scene and instruction; the toss rule only lowers scores). Nine reruns on this task.py were refused by the Dream API (DA-4000).
